blocks.body: The initial enrollment period runs seven months around your 65th birthday (three months before, the birthday month, three months after). Signing up late for Part B without other qualifying coverage brings a lifetime premium penalty, and COBRA, retiree or Marketplace coverage does not count: generally only coverage from your own or your spouse's current employment lets you delay Part B without it. Once you have Part A, Marketplace premium help ends, and the plan does not end on its own, so end it when Medicare starts. If you keep contributing to an HSA after 65, stop six months before you apply for Medicare or Social Security, because Part A coverage can reach back up to six months. Medigap's one-time open enrollment runs six months from when Part B starts at 65 or older; after it, insurers are generally allowed to refuse you or charge more for health problems, apart from certain protected cases and any extra state rights. Income in retirement also drives Medicare surcharges (IRMAA) with a two-year lookback; if stopping work cut your income, you can ask SSA to lower the surcharge. If income and savings are limited, Medicare Savings Programs and Extra Help can help pay premiums and drug costs.
blocks.plain: Your first chance to sign up for Medicare lasts seven months around your 65th birthday: three months before, your birthday month, and three months after. If you sign up late for Part B and had no other qualifying coverage, you pay a higher premium for life. COBRA, retiree or Marketplace coverage does not count: generally only coverage from your own or your spouse's current job lets you delay Part B without that penalty. Once you have Part A, you lose Marketplace savings. The Marketplace plan does not stop by itself, so end it when Medicare starts. If you keep putting money in an HSA after 65, stop six months before you apply for Medicare or Social Security, because Part A can start up to six months back. You get one six-month window to buy a Medigap policy, starting when Part B begins at 65 or older. After that, insurers can usually turn you down or charge more for health problems, except in some special cases or where your state gives you more rights. Your retirement income also sets extra Medicare charges (IRMAA), based on your income from two years earlier. If you stopped working and earn less now, you can ask Social Security to lower that charge. If your income and savings are small, Medicare Savings Programs and Extra Help can help pay premiums and drug costs.

blocks.body: Claiming at 62, full retirement age or 70 is one of the largest decisions most retirees make. Waiting, up to 70, raises the monthly check you get for life, and for a married higher earner, delaying also raises the survivor benefit. Claiming earlier can still be the right call if you need the income or your health suggests a shorter retirement. If you claim before full retirement age and keep working, benefits can be withheld when earnings pass a yearly limit; they are credited back in a recalculated check at full retirement age.
blocks.plain: Whether you claim at 62, at full retirement age, or at 70 is one of the biggest money choices most retirees make. Waiting, up to age 70, makes your monthly check bigger for the rest of your life. For a married person who earned more, waiting also raises what the surviving spouse would get. Claiming earlier can still make sense if you need the money now or your health points to a shorter retirement. If you claim before full retirement age and keep working, Social Security can hold back some payments when you earn over a yearly limit. It adds those months back into your check once you reach full retirement age.

blocks.body: Which accounts you draw first, and how much, shapes your lifetime tax bill and your sequence-of-returns exposure. If Social Security is your main income, this step matters less. The years between retiring and starting Social Security or RMDs are often the cheapest years for Roth conversions; plan withdrawals, the claim age and conversions together, since all three change the income that sets Medicare surcharges and Marketplace premium help.
blocks.plain: Which accounts you take money from first, and how much you take, shapes the taxes you pay over your life and how exposed you are to a bad run of early market returns. If Social Security is most of your income, this step matters less. The years after you stop working but before Social Security or required withdrawals begin are often the cheapest time to move money into a Roth account (a Roth conversion). Plan your withdrawals, when you claim Social Security, and any Roth conversions together, because all three change the income that sets extra Medicare charges and Marketplace premium help.

blocks.body: Required minimum distributions from traditional accounts start at age 73, or at 75 if you were born in 1960 or later. The first one can wait until April 1 of the next year, but then two fall in the same tax year; while you still work, a current employer's plan can usually wait until you retire. Qualified charitable distributions from an IRA (from age 70½) can satisfy RMDs without adding to income. Roth IRAs and Roth accounts in workplace plans have no RMDs while the owner is alive.
blocks.plain: Required minimum distributions from traditional accounts start at age 73, or at age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later. You can wait until April 1 of the next year for the first one, but then you take two in the same tax year. If you still work, you can usually wait on your current employer's plan until you retire. Giving straight from an IRA to charity (a qualified charitable distribution, allowed from age 70½) can count toward them without adding to your income. Roth IRAs and Roth accounts in workplace plans have no required withdrawals while the owner is alive.

blocks.body: About 70% of Americans turning 65 will need some long-term care, but more people get it at home than in facilities, and much of it is unpaid. Medicare and Medigap do not pay for this kind of care; Medicaid does if you meet your state's income, asset and care-need rules. Otherwise the decision is between insuring, self-funding, or a hybrid. A long-term care policy's price depends on your age when you buy, and premiums can rise after you buy.

new_claims.claim: A beneficiary under full retirement age whose earnings exceed the annual exempt amount has benefits withheld (the retirement earnings test); at full retirement age SSA recalculates the benefit to credit the withheld months
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 42 U.S.C. §403(b)(1) (deductions on account of work); SSA: 'If you are younger than full retirement age and earn more than the yearly earnings limit, we may reduce your benefit amount' and 'We will recalculate your benefit amount to give you credit for the months we reduced or withheld benefits'. The 2026 limit is not stated in the text. Added 2026-11-16 (ADV-40, CFP-43).

new_claims.claim: A Roth conversion is included in gross income, and the premium tax credit uses modified AGI (AGI plus nontaxable Social Security, tax-exempt interest and excluded foreign income), so withdrawals, the Social Security claim and conversions change the income that sets Marketplace premium help and IRMAA; the years before Social Security or RMDs are often lower-tax years for conversions
new_claims.note: Mechanics verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: §408A(d)(3)(A)(i) ('there shall be included in gross income any amount which would be includible were it not part of a qualified rollover contribution'; (C) treats a conversion as such a distribution); §36B(d)(2)(B) (MAGI definition). That the gap years are 'often the cheapest' for conversions is a planning convention, not law. Added 2026-11-16 (CFP-42, ADV-41).

new_claims.claim: RMDs begin at applicable age 73 for those attaining 72 after 2022 and 73 before 2033, and 75 for those attaining 74 after 2032 (everyone born in 1960 or later); the first RMD may be delayed to April 1 of the following year, putting two RMDs in that year; workplace-plan participants (not 5% owners) can delay until the year they retire; Roth IRAs and designated Roth accounts have no RMDs during the owner's life
new_claims.source: 26 U.S.C. §401(a)(9)(C)(i), (ii), (v); §408A(c)(4); IRS 'Retirement plan and IRA RMD FAQs'
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: §401(a)(9)(C)(v) (applicable age 73 / 75 clauses, quoted), §401(a)(9)(C)(i) (required beginning date April 1 following the later of attaining the applicable age or retiring), (C)(ii) (no still-working delay for 5% owners or IRAs), §408A(c)(4) (lifetime RMD rule does not apply to Roth IRAs); IRS FAQ Q3 (first RMD by April 1, second by Dec. 31 of the same year) and the Roth/designated Roth statement. The clauses overlap for 1959 births; the text names a birth year only for the 75 rule. Added 2026-11-16 (ADV-42, CFP-41).

new_claims.claim: Medicare and Medigap do not pay for long-term (custodial) care; Medicaid pays for custodial care in nursing homes and at home for people who meet their state's income and asset limits and its separate determination of need for long-term care services
new_claims.source: Medicare.gov 'Long-term care' coverage page (CMS); ACL/HHS LongTermCare.gov 'Medicaid'
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: Medicare.gov ('Medicare and most health insurance, including Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap), don't pay for long-term care services'); ACL ('Unlike Medicare, Medicaid does pay for custodial care in nursing homes and at home'; eligibility requires 'income and assets that do not exceed the levels used by your state'). Whether Medicaid pays for most long-term care nationally was not read. Added 2026-11-16 (ADV-43). Checker 2026-11-16: ACL also reads 'the state will make an additional determination of whether you qualify for long-term care services'; the text names the care-need test.

new_claims.claim: More people use long-term care at home than in facilities, and unpaid-only care at home is the most common form; long-term care insurance cost depends on age at purchase, and the insurer can raise premiums beyond the pre-set amount
new_claims.source: ACL/HHS LongTermCare.gov 'How much care will you need?' and 'Long-term care insurance costs'
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: ACL ('more people use long-term care services at home (and for longer) than in facilities'; table: unpaid care only, 59% of users); ACL costs page ('the insurance company can increase your premiums beyond the pre-set amount'; cost varies by 'your age at the time of purchase'). ACL pages last modified 2020-02-18; the underlying study is older than CL066's 2022 ASPE source. Added 2026-11-16 (ADV-43, CFP-44).

owner_decisions.what: Add a retirement step on choosing the pension payout form (lump sum or annuity; single-life or joint-and-survivor; spousal consent).
owner_decisions.why_owner: Adds a new step to the retirement playbook, which changes the product's shape. Many readers have no defined-benefit pension, so the owner should decide whether the step belongs in the main flow or behind a condition.

draft.title: Choose how your pension pays out
draft.when: Before your pension paperwork is due
draft.body: If you have a pension, choose between a lump sum, if the plan offers one, and monthly payments, and between payments for your life only or joint-and-survivor payments. In most private-employer pensions, if you are married, the default is a joint-and-survivor annuity, and choosing anything else generally needs your spouse's written consent, witnessed by a notary or plan representative; government plans set their own rules. Ask the plan whether the choice can change after payments start; in plans PBGC pays, it cannot after the first payment.
draft.plain: If you have a pension, you choose how it pays out: one lump sum, if your plan offers it, or monthly checks, paid for your life only or for both your life and your spouse's. In most pensions from private employers, if you are married, the standard choice is payments that keep going to your spouse after you die. To pick anything else, your spouse usually must agree in writing, signed in front of a notary or a plan representative. Government pensions have their own rules. Ask the plan if you can change your mind after payments start. In plans run by PBGC, you cannot change it after the first payment.

new_claim.claim: For a married participant in a private-employer defined benefit or money purchase plan covered by ERISA the default payout is a qualified joint and survivor annuity; electing another form requires the spouse's written consent witnessed by a plan representative or notary; ERISA's Title I does not apply to governmental plans; in PBGC-paid plans the benefit form cannot be changed after the first payment
new_claim.source: 29 U.S.C. §1055(a), (c)(2); §1003(b)(1); DOL/EBSA FAQ; PBGC 'Pension benefits overview'
new_claim.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 29 U.S.C. §1055(c)(2)(A) (spousal written consent, 'witnessed by a plan representative or a notary public'); 29 U.S.C. §1003(b)(1) ('shall not apply to any employee benefit plan if— (1) such plan is a governmental plan'); DOL/EBSA FAQ, full page read by the checker ('In a defined benefit or money purchase plan, unless you and your spouse choose otherwise, the form of payment will include a survivor's benefit'); PBGC ('After the date of your first payment, you cannot change your selection'). Whether private plans generally allow a change after payments start was not read; the draft says 'ask the plan'. Drafted 2026-11-16 (CFP-39).

owner_decisions.what: Add a first retirement step for people stopping work before 65: plan health coverage until Medicare (COBRA or the Marketplace), noting that the income taken changes Marketplace premium help.
owner_decisions.why_owner: Adds a new step, and the playbook assumes retirement at 65. The owner should decide whether early retirees get a conditional first step or a pointer to the job-loss coverage step.

draft.title: If you retire before 65, plan coverage until Medicare
draft.body: If you stop working before 65, line up health coverage until Medicare starts. Losing job-based coverage opens a Marketplace special enrollment period, and COBRA is another bridge. Marketplace premium help is based on the household income you report, so traditional IRA or 401(k) withdrawals, Roth conversions and capital gains can change what you pay.
draft.plain: If you stop working before 65, plan how you will have health insurance until Medicare starts. Losing your job's coverage lets you sign up for a Marketplace plan outside the usual sign-up season, and COBRA is another option. Help with Marketplace premiums depends on the household income you report, so taking money from a traditional IRA or 401(k), Roth conversions and selling investments at a gain can change what you pay.

new_claim.claim: Losing minimum essential coverage (for example job-based coverage) triggers a Marketplace special enrollment period; the premium tax credit is based on household modified AGI; traditional retirement-account withdrawals, Roth conversions and capital gains are included in gross income
